newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi ruler's main rival pessimist on future.
newsitem.headline: Burundi ruler's main rival pessimist on future.

text.p: The main Tutsi rival of Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya said on Monday an army coup has failed to bring peace to the tiny African country and an end to vicious civil war was a long way off.
In another development, five members of the Hutu-dominated Frodebu party including Hutu rebel leader Leonard Nyangoma said they were taking control of the party and backed armed struggle.
Former Tutsi military ruler Jean-Baptise Bagaza, deposed by Buyoya in his first coup in 1987, said a military solution to Burundi's problems was possible but would prove too costly.
"I am a pessimist," he told Reuters at his villa overlooking the capital Bujumbura. "I think that before the coup we were on the edge of a precipice, and now we have gone over it."
Bagaza said his Parena party wanted a conference to bring all protagonists together and to reunite the divided country.
Buyoya, who seized power from Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya in a July 25 coup by the Tutsi-dominated army, says he cannot negotiate with Hutu rebels unless they lay down their arms.
"Other solutions are possible, the violent solutions, continuing the war, but I say that is too expensive, for everyone," Bagaza said.
Fears are widespread that Burundi might go the way of its northern neighbour Rwanda, where up to a million people were killed in genocide and three months of civil war in 1994.
Bagaza said some form of power-sharing would be needed to satisfy Tutsis, who control the state apparatus and the army although they comprise only 15 percent of the population.

He said there was a way to approach democracy for Burundi along the lines of that practised in the West "but the political establishment in Burundi has to accept sharing power (with the Hutu majority)".
Buyoya deposed Bagaza -- who himself seized power in a coup -- in 1987 and began a transition to democracy which led to democratic elections in 1993.
Frodebu party won those polls, but the elected president was assassinated by Tutsi troops, triggering the massacres of an estimated 50,000 Tutsis and Hutus across the country.

Buyoya, who says he is more of a democrat than his rivals, has said his military-appointed government will rule for a transitional period of three years. Last week he lifted bans on political parties and parliament imposed after he seized power.
Bagaza said unless there was open talks between enemies, killings would continue to tear at the heart of the country.
"Before the rebels just had machetes. Now they have mortars. Next year they will have more," he said.
Buyoya's leadership said on Sunday it would stick to its programme even if it did not win an immediate end to sanctions imposed by regional states in retaliation for the army coup.
In a statement, five surviving members of Frodebu's eight -person Stautary Executive Committee including Nyangoma, who is in exile, said they were taking over the party leadership.
Ntibantunganya, who is a member of the committee and has been holed up at the U.S. ambassador's residence in Bujumbura since shortly before the coup, did not sign the statement.
They said they would elect a president as soon as possible and condemned the army coup and the military for assassinating national and local Frodebu officials and killing civilians.
They said it was vital to restore constitutional rule and democracy in Burundi through negotiations or by continuing the military and political struggle as legitimate defence.
No comment was available from Frodebu leader Jean Minani.
